name: Lisu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Bradley, David 2003/2017. 'Lisu', in Thurgood & LaPolla (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages. Routledge. (phonology chapter plausibly covering prosody; paywalled)

sources.citation: Hope, Edward R. 1974. The deep syntax of Lisu sentences: a transformational case grammar. Pacific Linguistics B-34. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-B34
sources.note: Orthography/phonology note pp. vi-viii: suprasegmentals posited are palatalisation, labialisation, laryngealisation and five tones; stress not listed. p.12: in Lisu focus is marked by linear order, whereas in English phonological stress marks focus. p.155: 'a morphophonemic rule adds stress to the particular verb... being negated' (contrastive/sentence level). No word-stress placement rule.

sources.citation: Hope, Edward R. 1971. Problems of phone assignment in the description of Thailand Lisu phonology. In W. Glover, M. Hari & E. R. Hope (eds), Papers in South East Asian Linguistics No. 2, 53-78. Pacific Linguistics A-29. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-A29.53
sources.note: Southern (Thailand) Lisu. Sec. 4 'Problems of assignment of suprasegmentals' covers tone and laryngealisation only. Stress appears only in passing: p.58 an on-glide allophone of /zY/ is the only one 'in all unstressed syllables'; pp.62-63 nasalisation of [h]-initial syllables tends to disappear 'in syllables with mid tone when these have other than primary stress'. No statement of where stress falls.

sources.citation: Fraser, James Outram. 1922. Handbook of the Lisu (Yawyin) language. Rangoon: Superintendent, Government Printing, Burma.
sources.note: Central Lisu (Tengyueh). Describes sounds and six tones; p.5: 'No attempt has been made to represent accentuation, this being best learnt from the lips of the natives.' Explicitly declines to describe stress.

sources.citation: Yu, Defen. 2007. Aspects of Lisu phonology and grammar, a language of Southeast Asia. Pacific Linguistics 588. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU. xvii+254 pp. (ANU Open Research handle 1885/146286)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: Harvard print copy (Scan & Deliver or loan): WID Offsite Storage PL4001.L61 Y8 2007
sources.note: Image-only scan; ch.1 and ch.3 (Phonology, pp.27-80) scanned. Ch.3 compares five PRC dialects (Shibacha, Nujiang, Ninglang, Dechang, Lipo): syllable structure CVT, six tones (Ninglang 5, Lipo 4), inventories, allophony, sandhi. No section and no sentence on stress/accent (scanned grep for stress/accent/prominence: zero hits).

sources.citation: Stanley, Rael. 2023. Acoustic phonetics of Northern Lisu: vowels, tones, and fricatives. PhD thesis, La Trobe University. doi:10.26181/25447858.v1
sources.note: Acoustic study of Northern Lisu vowels, tones, fricatives; text search finds no statement about Lisu word stress or prominence (only CPP and English-stress references).

sources.citation: Tabain, Marija, David Bradley & Defen Yu. 2019. Central Lisu. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 49(1): 129-147. doi:10.1017/S0025100318000129
sources.note: JIPA Illustration of Central (literary) Lisu: sections Consonants, Clusters, Vowels, Tones (f0 plots, durations, sandhi, clitic fusion), transcribed passage. No prosody/stress section; no statement on word stress.

sources.citation: Li, Na. 2017. Tonal patterns of Lisu language. Proceedings of ESSAEME 2017 (Advances in Social Science, Education and Humanities Research 119), 208-212. Atlantis Press. doi:10.2991/essaeme-17.2017.42
sources.note: Acoustic description of the six Nujiang Lisu tones (pitch, duration, phonation); silent on stress.

sources.citation: Bradley, David, with Edward Reginald Hope, James Fish and Maya Bradley. 2006. Southern Lisu Dictionary. STEDT Monograph Series 4. Berkeley: Sino-Tibetan Etymological Dictionary and Thesaurus Project. xxxiv+346 pp.
sources.note: Southern Lisu. Introduction phonology (pp. xx-xxiv): initials, vowels, six tones, prefix tone reversal, two-tone sequences on sentence-final markers 'somewhat longer than a single syllable'. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1994. A dictionary of the northern dialect of Lisu (China and Southeast Asia). Pacific Linguistics C-126. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C126
sources.note: Northern Lisu. Introduction (pp. viii-x) gives consonants, ten vowels, six tones, tone sandhi in four-syllable compounds; nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Rose, Archibald & J. Coggin Brown. 1910. Lisu (Yawyin) tribes of the Burma-China frontier. Memoirs of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 3(4): 249-277.
sources.note: Ethnographic memoir with vocabulary; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 2003. Lisu. In G. Thurgood & R. J. LaPolla (eds), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 222-235. London: Routledge; revised in 2nd ed. 2017 (Routledge Language Family Series).

sources.access_detail: publisher DOI, paywalled; Harvard e-access not checked
sources.note: The standard modern sketch by the main Lisu specialist; its phonology section is the most likely place for an explicit remark on stress/rhythm (e.g. prefix a- reduction, clitic fusion) that the dictionaries and JIPA piece omit. Named by the earlier scan as the unreachable source.
